resources.string: Draws the notification light above the lock screen. No screen content is read, and notification titles and message text are never read.

To see your notifications as a light, the app needs notification access. It only learns which app posted, when, and the counter that app publishes \u2014 it never reads titles or message text. Enable it now?
No setting matches your search. Try one short word, for example brightness, count or night.
The master switch, and the moments in which the light may appear at all.
What the light looks like: its shape, its movement, its color, and how much of the screen is blacked out.
How long one light lasts, and the settings that trade brightness and smoothness against battery.
Which apps may light up, and the times and phone states in which the light stays off.
For phones without an always-on panel, plus the test light and the debug log.

The main always-on light: it glows while the display is off or in the phone\u2019s own always-on mode, for the light duration set below. Notifications that arrive while you use the phone are saved and shown the next time the screen goes off.

On by default: the whole display is covered with black, so nothing of the phone\u2019s own always-on screen shows through. Turn this off to cover only the top two thirds and leave the bottom third exactly as the phone draws it. Touches always pass through, so the fingerprint sensor and any shortcuts down there keep working \u2014 you just cannot see them. Applies to every style.

Keeps the light visible when you wake the phone but it is still locked, for example after a single press of the power button. Waking the screen is not an unlock: the light stays until you unlock the phone or the light duration ends.
Two quick taps anywhere wake the phone. This works on the fallback dark canvas below, because only that canvas can receive touches.

Leave this OFF if your phone has its own always-on display. It is only for phones that show nothing when the display is off: it opens a very dim black screen so the light has something to sit on. That screen keeps the panel awake, just like \u201cKeep the panel awake for the dark screen\u201d below, which is the switch to use if you want that for brightness reasons. The power button still turns the display off. With both off, the light and the black background are drawn without waking anything.

Unlocking the phone hides the light. With this on, turning the display off or locking the phone again brings the light back for any notification you have not dismissed. Dismissed notifications never light up again.
Fewer redraws per second while the light moves. The animation looks slightly less smooth and the phone does noticeably less work. No effect on the still app icons.

Turns the whole light slowly on and off instead of keeping it on: the two numbers below say how many seconds it is on and how many it is off. Saves battery on panels that cannot dim themselves. The light duration above still ends it.

Used when the style above is set to \u201cApp icons\u201d. The icons of the apps that have a notification are shown on the black screen instead of a ring, edge or dot. They are completely still: nothing pulses, flashes or blinks, and the screen is redrawn only when the icons move. With no notification the screen stays completely black. The icons belong to the dark always-on screen; while the phone is awake on the lock screen its own clock is left alone.

App icon is the colourful picture you tap on the home screen: familiar, but busy at small sizes. Notification icon is the small symbol the app itself puts in the status bar \u2014 a flat, simple shape made to stay readable when tiny, so all icons look like one family. With \u201cOriginal colors\u201d, a notification symbol is filled with the color that app chose for its own notifications; if it chose none, the color is taken from its app icon, and a very dark color is brightened so it stays visible on black. White and black work the same for both. If an app has no status-bar symbol, its app icon is used instead. A few apps use a plain generic symbol, so those can look alike.

Original colors keeps an app icon as it is, and fills a notification symbol with that app\u2019s own color. White turns each icon into a light monochrome glyph, which is the calmest look on a black screen. Black is the inverted form and is always drawn on a light plate so it stays visible.
How large each app icon is drawn, from 18 dp (small and unobtrusive) to 96 dp (easy to see from across the room).
Draws a rounded plate behind every icon, which helps icons with transparent or busy artwork stand out. Black icons always get a light plate, whatever this switch says.

A still image can burn into an OLED panel. With this on, the icon block is placed a few pixels differently for every light-up and moves again after ten minutes, so no pixel stays lit in the same place. Nothing slides around while you look at it: it stays in one spot for the whole time the icons are shown. Turn it off only if you want the icons pinned to one spot.

Where the icons sit on the dark screen. The icons are laid out in rows; these settings decide where the block of rows starts, how far apart the icons are and how many go into one row. Everything applies to the always-on screen only, and the icons never leave the panel: an offset that would push them off the edge is limited to the edge.
On: every row is centered on the screen, which is the calmest look. Off: the rows start at the left edge, and the horizontal offset below decides how far from that edge.
Moves the whole block left (negative) or right (positive). With centering on, 0 means exactly in the middle; with centering off, 0 means at the left edge.

What the vertical offset is measured from. \u201cBelow the camera\u201d keeps the icons clear of the camera and the status bar. \u201cTop of the screen\u201d measures from the very top, so 0 puts the icons at the top edge. \u201cBottom of the screen\u201d measures upwards from the bottom edge to the bottom of the last row.
Distance from the anchor chosen above. Larger values move the icons down, except with the bottom anchor, where they move the icons up.
Icons per row: %1$d (0 = fill the width)
0 fits as many icons into one row as the screen width allows. A fixed number gives a predictable shape: 1 is a vertical list, 2 or 3 is a narrow block. More icons wrap into the next row.
Empty space between neighbours. Bigger gaps are easier to tell apart at a glance; 0 packs the icons tightly next to each other.
One icon per app, newest app first. Apps beyond this limit are not drawn, which keeps a busy notification list from filling the whole screen.
When the last row has fewer icons than the others: on centers that row on its own, off lines it up with the column above it. Only has an effect while horizontal centering is on.
Keep icons inside the black area

On: rows that would reach past the blacked-out part of the screen are dropped, so nothing is drawn over the area that is deliberately left untouched. Off: the icons may use the whole panel, including the lower part \u2014 useful if you moved them down on purpose.
Icon position back to the defaults
Shows how many notifications are waiting in each app as a number below its icon. The number is part of the same still image: it does not blink and it moves with the icons.

Prints the count under each app icon. A single notification shows no number unless the switch below is on, so a quiet screen stays quiet. Counts above 99 are shown as \u201c99+\u201d. Room for the number is reserved, so rows never overlap it. It counts notifications, not messages: an app that bundles five messages into one notification shows 1, and posting a notification with the same tag again replaces it instead of adding one.

\u201CNotifications\u201D counts how many notifications an app has posted. \u201CThe app\u2019s own counter\u201D uses the number the app itself publishes, which for a messenger is usually its unread messages \u2014 so five messages bundled into one notification show 5 instead of 1. Apps publish this voluntarily: if an app sends no counter, or sends 0, the plain notification count is used instead. The number shown is never lower than the number of notifications, so an app that always writes 1 cannot hide that three are waiting. The counter of an app\u2019s summary notification is read too, because that is often the only place the total appears.
Add up the counters of several notifications

Only relevant when an app has more than one notification and each carries a counter. Off takes the highest counter, which is right for apps that repeat their overall total on every notification. On adds them up, which is right for apps that count per conversation. If the number looks doubled, turn this off; if it looks too small, turn it on.
On: every icon gets a number, even when the app has only one notification. Off: the number appears from two notifications upwards.
Draws the number on a small dark rounded badge instead of straight onto the black screen. Slightly easier to read next to bright icons; it also makes the block a little taller.

Ongoing notifications that cannot be swiped away: players, downloads, navigation -- and phone calls. A call counts when it is tagged as a call, when it takes over the screen (an incoming call does), or when it uses the system call layout. The AOSP dialer tags only its incoming call, so its ongoing call is covered by the app list below, which already contains your dialer. That list is used by the \u201cAllow calls + selected apps\u201d choice. The app filter above still applies: an app excluded there never lights up.

How long one light lasts after the last notification, from 1 minute to 3 hours. The slider snaps to fixed steps, so a useful value is always one tap away. When the time is up the screen goes completely black until the next notification arrives. A longer time costs more battery.
Always-on brightness: same as the phone
Keep the panel awake for the dark screen

Off by default, and best left off: the panel then dozes, which is by far the cheapest, and the power button is never contested. On: while a light is showing, the dark screen asks the display to stay awake instead of dozing. An awake display uses normal brightness \u2014 the phone\u2019s own setting, slider included. It costs more battery: a dozing panel refreshes itself and lets the phone sleep, an awake one keeps the display pipeline running. The light\u2019s duration still ends it, the power button still turns the display off, and with no notification nothing is woken at all. Some phones refuse to stay awake here; the app notices, lets go at once and leaves the panel dozing for a while instead of fighting them. After a power-button press it also stays dozing for a short moment, so the button always wins. Off: the panel dozes, which is much cheaper, but the phone then pins its own fixed always-on brightness. On LCD screens leaving this off is usually the better choice.

Needs \u201cKeep the panel awake\u201d above. On: the always-on screen asks for no brightness of its own, so the phone decides \u2014 it is then exactly as bright as the lock screen and follows the brightness slider live, adaptive brightness included. Off: the brightness set below is used instead, whatever the system slider says. The two cannot be combined: any brightness an app asks for takes the panel off the system slider.

The panel dozes: cheapest, but the phone pins its own fixed always-on brightness there and following the system slider is impossible. The brightness below is requested instead \u2014 some phones clamp it, and a few ignore it completely. If moving the slider below changes nothing, the brightness of the dark screen is set by the phone itself: look in the phone\u2019s settings under Lock screen or Always-on display for its own brightness control.
The panel stays awake and the dark screen uses the brightness below, independent of the system slider.
Adaptive brightness is on, and the always-on screen follows it just like every other screen.
Adaptive brightness is off, so the always-on screen follows the brightness slider directly.

Used whenever the phone\u2019s brightness is not being followed: this is then the brightness of the dark screen itself, 100% being full brightness and 40% a comfortable night level. An awake panel usually honours it; on a dozing panel some phones clamp it to their own always-on level and a few ignore it completely. Higher brightness also means more battery and more burn-in risk.
No cutout reported \u2014 using fallback position
